The original names for these columns were "data.bug_id", "data.version", "data.product", "data.component", "assigned_to" (which I split into assigned_user & assigned_name), "data.bug_severity", "data.bug_status", "data.short_desc", "data.creation_ts", and "data.delta_ts."

Also, here is my rough code for the function itself:

```r
#' Parse bugzilla from Perceval
#'
#' @param perceval_path path to perceval binary
#' @param bugzilla_link link to specific bugzilla site
#' @param save_path optional save path for .rds object
#' @export
#' @family parsers
parse_bugzilla <- function(perceval_path,bugzilla_link,date,save_path=NA){
 
  # Expand paths (e.g. "~/Desktop" => "/Users/someuser/Desktop")
  perceval_path <- path.expand(perceval_path)
  save_path <- ifelse(!is.na(save_path),path.expand(save_path),NA)

  # Parsed JSON output. 
  # Matches command in perceval to get bugzilla data via the traditional backend
  perceval_output <- system2(perceval_path,
                             args = c('bugzilla',bugzilla_link,'--json-line','--from-date',date),
                             stdout = TRUE,
                             stderr = FALSE)

  # Create the data.table from JSON output
  perceval_parsed <- data.table(jsonlite::stream_in(textConnection(perceval_output),verbose = FALSE))

  # To learn about the data
  # print(names(perceval_parsed))
  
  # Here, I take the most relevant columns of information (other columns get dropped)
  # There are a lot of 1x1 dataframes that must be unlisted first, which is done here
  perceval_parsed <- perceval_parsed[, .(bug_id=unlist(data.bug_id), 
                                          version=unlist(data.version),
                                          component=unlist(data.component),
                                          product=unlist(data.product),
                                          severity=unlist(data.bug_severity),
                                          status=unlist(data.bug_status),
                                          summary=unlist(data.short_desc),
                                          date_created=unlist(data.creation_ts),
                                          date_modified=unlist(data.delta_ts),
                                          data.assigned_to = data.assigned_to
                                         )
                                        ]
  
  # Unlisting other columns which are not 1x1 dataframes and need more work
  perceval_parsed <- perceval_parsed[, .(
                                          assigned_user=unlist(data.assigned_to[[1]]["__text__"]),
                                          # Set name field to NA if the name isn't found
                                      assigned_name=append(unlist(data.assigned_to[[1]]),NA)[2]),,
                                                                                              by=list(
                                                                                                bug_id,
                                                                                                version,
                                                                                              product,
                                                                                              component,
                                                                                              severity,
                                                                                              status,
                                                                                              summary,
                                                                                              date_created,
                                                                                              date_modified)]
                                     
  
  # Reorder the columns in a sensible format
  perceval_parsed <- data.table::setcolorder(perceval_parsed, c("bug_id", "version", "product", "component", "assigned_user", "assigned_name", "severity","status", "summary", "date_created", "date_modified"))

  #Parsing bugzilla can take a while, save if a path is provided
   if(!is.na(save_path)){
     saveRDS(perceval_parsed,save_path)
   }
  return(perceval_parsed)
}

```

#'  Download Bugzilla issues and comments using the Bugzilla REST API
#'
#' @param bugzilla_site link to specific bugzilla site
#' @param start_timestamp when to start bug retrieval (ex. 2023-01-01T00:14:57Z)
#' @param end_timestamp when to end bug retrieval (ex. 2023-01-01T00:14:57Z)
#' @param project_name the name of the bugzilla project (ex. redhat for https://bugzilla.redhat.com")
#' @param comments whether to download comments
#' @export
download_bugzilla_from_rest_api <- function(bugzilla_site, start_timestamp, end_timestamp, project_name, comments=FALSE){
  # Format link to retrieve data using Bugzilla REST API
  bugzilla_site <- paste(bugzilla_site, "/rest", sep="")
  
  # Get the issues starting from the specified date
  issues <- httr::GET(paste(bugzilla_site, "/bug", "?creation_time=", start_timestamp, sep=""))
  json_issues <- rawToChar(issues$content)
  
  # Get table for the bug issues
  bug_issue_table <- data.table(jsonlite::stream_in(textConnection(json_issues),verbose = FALSE))
  
  # Get table in actual table format
  table <- data.table(bug_issue_table[["bugs"]][[1]])
  
  # Filter the table to only include bugs within date range
  filtered_issue_table <- table[table$creation_time <= end_timestamp]
  
  # Get the bug ids. Needed to know which comments to retrieve.
  bug_ids <- filtered_issue_table[["id"]]
  
  # Download the comments if user wants them
  json_comments <- vector()
  if (comments == TRUE){
    # Get the comments associated with the bugs acquired
    for (bug in bug_ids){
      comments <- httr::GET(paste(bugzilla_site, "/bug/", bug, "/comment", sep=""))
      json_comments <- c(json_comments, rawToChar(comments$content))
    }
  }
  
  # List to hold the issues and comments
  json_issues_comments <- list()
  
  json_issues_comments[["issues"]] <- jsonlite::toJSON(filtered_issue_table)
  json_issues_comments[["comments"]] <- jsonlite::toJSON(lapply(json_comments, jsonlite::fromJSON))
  
  
  # Save issues and comments

You want to ensure your unit tests do not require the user to download data in a specific path. They should test what comes on a git clone of Kaiaulu repo, or any assumptions states on the README that the user should follow. 

One difficulty with that is, for example, if you are testing one of the parse functions. For example, `parse_gitlog` since you need a .git file to test them. To that end, I created two functions for you to see how you could go about it. In essence, you want to write a function to SetUp and TearDown the unit tests, by making some mockup lightweight data when the function is called.

This is exactly what the new two functions do. They are fairly simple, and only really perform a set of command line commands via system2 to create a file, add it and make a commit. 

Please use this pair of functions for unit tests associated to git log. Creating a mockup parse_mbox() function is more elaborated, so if your function tests columns on parse_mbox() for example, please map your unit test to test the equivalent on parse_gitlog instead. 

 I did a few quick tests of the function pair on my end, but if you run into any issues let me know. 

A similar idea applies if you are testing something like a project configuration file. You would need to create a sample project configuration file on the fly to then test functions for it. In practice, however, it suffices to test the parameters parse_gitlog() takes directly, since reading from the config files is very simple. 

## Hardcoding filepaths

Remember your test functions should assume a tools.yml exists where it currently is on the git repo in Kaiaulu. If you are testing someone placed Perceval in the correct place, or any other tool, you have to read it from the tools.yml so when the user downloads Kaiaulu, it properly test where they specified it is. If you hardcode the path instead, you are not taking into account the user input, and nothing is being tested.

## Descriptive Names for Tests

Try to be very specific in the description of testthat. When all tests are run, the description should give enough intuition of what you are trying to test and what you expected. Some unit tests only mention what were being tested, but not what was being expected. 

## Precise Assertions 

Try to refine the tests to specific assumptions by asserting equal rather than "return error". For example, if you expect a user to use a version of Perceval, assert equal to the version number the test expects, rather than "something went wrong" when return_error() is used. The assert equals then becomes further documentation of the function, on what behavior it should have given a very specific input.
